skin_diseases.name: Tinea Corporis (Ringworm)
skin_diseases.description: A dermatophyte fungal infection of the body skin presenting as ring-shaped, scaly, itchy rashes. Extremely common in India due to hot and humid climate, often misdiagnosed and mistreated with steroid creams, leading to Tinea Incognito.
symptoms: Ring-shaped red rash with raised border
Central clearing
Intense itching, especially at night
Scaly, flaky skin
Multiple expanding rings
Worsened after steroid application (TI)
Commonly on thighs, buttocks, abdomen, arms
treatments: Topical antifungals (clotrimazole, miconazole, terbinafine, luliconazole) for 2-4 weeks
Oral antifungals for extensive/resistant disease: terbinafine 250mg daily 2-4 weeks OR itraconazole 100mg twice daily for 2-4 weeks
Luliconazole cream once daily (newer, effective against resistant tinea)
Avoid steroid-containing combination creams (major problem in India)
prevention: Change and wash clothes daily in hot weather
warning_signs: Not improving after 2 weeks of antifungal

skin_diseases.name: Tinea Cruris (Jock Itch)
skin_diseases.description: Dermatophyte fungal infection of the groin, inner thighs, and buttocks. Extremely common in Indian men due to heat, humidity, and tight synthetic clothing. Often called 'dhobi itch' locally.
symptoms: Red, itchy rash in groin crease and inner thighs
Ring-shaped border with clearing in center
Flaking, cracking skin
Burning sensation
Worsens with sweat and activity
Usually spares scrotum (unlike Candidal intertrigo)
May extend to buttocks
treatments: Topical antifungals (clotrimazole, terbinafine, miconazole) twice daily for 2-4 weeks
Keep area dry and clean
Oral antifungals for recurrent/extensive: terbinafine or itraconazole
Antifungal powder (miconazole or zinc oxide based) to maintain dryness
Treat concurrent tinea pedis
warning_signs: Extending to scrotum or penis (consider Candida)
Not responding to antifungals (rule out erythrasma)

skin_diseases.name: Tinea Versicolor (Pityriasis Versicolor)
skin_diseases.description: A common superficial yeast infection caused by Malassezia species, presenting as hypopigmented (lighter) or hyperpigmented (darker) patches, particularly noticeable in dark-skinned Indians. Very prevalent in tropical India.
causes: Malassezia furfur / M. globosa (part of normal flora, overgrowth in certain conditions)
symptoms: Multiple small scaly patches
Hypopigmented (lighter than surrounding skin) in dark-skinned individuals — most noticeable in Indians
Hyperpigmented (darker) patches in lighter-skinned
Fine powdery scale when scratched
Patches on upper trunk, shoulders, neck, upper arms
Minimal itching
Patches fail to tan in summer
treatments: Topical: Ketoconazole shampoo/cream or selenium sulfide shampoo, apply 15-20 min then wash off, daily for 2 weeks
Terbinafine spray or cream once daily for 2 weeks
Oral (for extensive/recurrent): Itraconazole 200mg daily for 5-7 days OR fluconazole 300-400mg single dose
Repigmentation takes weeks-months after treatment — sun exposure helps
prevention: Reduce sun exposure to sweating conditions
Use antifungal shampoo as body wash in summer

skin_diseases.name: Scabies
skin_diseases.description: A highly contagious skin infestation by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. Extremely common in India — entire families and communities affected. Causes intense, characteristic nocturnal itching. Often overcrowded living conditions contribute to spread in India.
causes: Sarcoptes scabiei mite burrows into skin to lay eggs
symptoms: Intense itching — dramatically worse at night
Fine, irregular burrow lines in skin (most diagnostic)
Small red bumps (papules), vesicles, or pustules
Rash between fingers (finger webspaces — classic)
Wrists, elbows, axillae, belt area, buttocks, genitals in adults
Infants: face, scalp, soles also affected
Secondary bacterial infection (impetigo) common from scratching
Same symptom pattern in multiple family members — highly suggestive
treatments: First line: Permethrin 5% cream — apply from neck down to all skin including under nails, leave 8-14 hours then wash off. Repeat after 7 days.
Alternative: Ivermectin 200mcg/kg orally, repeat after 7-14 days
Treat ALL household members simultaneously, same day
Wash all clothing, bedding in hot water (60°C) or seal in bag for 72 hours
Antihistamines for itch relief
Antibiotic if secondary bacterial infection
prevention: Avoid close skin contact with infected individuals
Wash clothing and bedding in hot water
warning_signs: Not responding to treatment (consider resistance or reinfection)

skin_diseases.name: Acne Vulgaris
skin_diseases.description: Common inflammatory skin condition of pilosebaceous units, extremely common in Indian adolescents and adults. Indian skin (type IV-VI) tends towards hyperpigmentation and post-inflammatory dark marks (PIH) after acne resolution, which is a major concern for patients.
causes: Indian dietary habits (high glycaemic load, dairy)
Humidity and pollution in Indian cities
symptoms: Blackheads (open comedones)
Whiteheads (closed comedones)
Papules (red bumps)
Pustules (pus-filled)
Nodules and cysts (severe)
Oily skin
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (dark marks) — very common in Indian skin
Scarring in severe/untreated cases
treatments: Mild: Benzoyl peroxide 2.5-5%, salicylic acid 0.5-2% face wash, adapalene 0.1% gel at night
Moderate: Topical clindamycin 1% + adapalene, oral doxycycline/minocycline
Severe/Nodular: Oral isotretinoin (Reticutan/Acutret) under dermatologist supervision
PIH (dark marks): Niacinamide, kojic acid, azelaic acid 15-20%, topical glycolic acid
PCOS-related acne: Address hormonal cause (oral contraceptives, spironolactone)
prevention: Gentle cleansing twice daily (avoid harsh scrubbing)
Sun protection (SPF 30+) daily — prevents PIH worsening
Avoid picking/squeezing — worsens PIH and scarring
warning_signs: Acne in neonates or older adults (underlying cause)

skin_diseases.name: Eczema / Atopic Dermatitis
skin_diseases.description: A chronic inflammatory skin condition causing intense itching and dry, inflamed skin. Common in India particularly in urban areas with pollution and changing allergen exposures. Often associated with asthma and allergic rhinitis (atopic triad).
causes: Environmental allergens (dust mites, pollen, pet dander)
Food allergens (milk, egg, wheat, nuts, fish)
symptoms: Intense itching (day and night)
Red, inflamed patches
Dry, scaly skin
Lichenification (thickened leather-like skin from chronic scratching)
Vesicles and weeping in acute flares
Typical distribution: elbow/knee creases, face (infants), neck, wrists, ankles
Secondary infections common from scratching
treatments: Emollients (moisturisers): cornerstone — apply multiple times daily to moist skin immediately after bathing (Vaseline, CeraVe, Cetaphil, shea butter)
Topical corticosteroids for flares: hydrocortisone (mild), betamethasone (moderate)
Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) for face and sensitive areas
Antihistamines for itch and sleep
Wet wrap therapy for severe flares
Dupilumab (biologic) for severe eczema unresponsive to topicals
Oral steroids short-term for acute severe flares
Treat infections with antibiotics
prevention: Use mild, fragrance-free soaps and laundry products
warning_signs: Signs of skin infection (warmth, pus, crusting)

skin_diseases.name: Psoriasis
skin_diseases.description: Chronic autoimmune inflammatory skin disease with rapid skin cell turnover causing thick, silvery-scaled plaques on red bases. Prevalence 0.5-2.3% in India. Often associated with psoriatic arthritis. Can significantly impair quality of life due to visibility.
causes: Autoimmune — T-cell mediated attack on skin
Triggers: stress, infection (Streptococcal throat — guttate psoriasis)
symptoms: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery-white scales
Itching and burning
Characteristic sites: scalp, elbows, knees, lower back
Nail changes: pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop sign
Scalp involvement very common — thick scale, hair loss
Psoriatic arthritis: joint pain and swelling in ~30%
Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding when scale removed
treatments: Topical: Corticosteroids (betamethasone), coal tar, vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol), salicylic acid for scalp
Phototherapy: Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) — widely available in India
Systemic: Methotrexate 7.5-25mg weekly (most used in India)
Acitretin, cyclosporin for severe disease
Biologic agents (adalimumab, etanercept, secukinumab, ixekizumab) for severe/resistant — expensive in India
Coal tar and salicylic acid shampoo for scalp psoriasis
prevention: Stress management (yoga, meditation — important in India)
warning_signs: Erythrodermic psoriasis (>90% body involvement — medical emergency)

skin_diseases.name: Vitiligo
skin_diseases.description: An autoimmune condition causing loss of melanocytes resulting in white patches. Affects approximately 1-2% of Indians — among the highest prevalence globally. Has major psychosocial impact in India due to social stigma and association (historically) with leprosy.
causes: Vitamin B12 and Vitamin D deficiency
Chemical exposure (phenols in rubber gloves, paints)
symptoms: Well-defined white macules and patches
Milky-white color with distinct borders
Any body site — around eyes, mouth, genitals, hands most common
May show Koebner phenomenon (new patches at injury sites)
White hair in affected patches (leukotrichia)
Increased sensitivity to sunburn
Usually asymptomatic — no pain or itch
treatments: Sun protection mandatory (high SPF — depigmented skin burns easily and lacks UV-protective melanin)
Topical corticosteroids (first line for localised, non-facial)
Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) for face and children
Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy — most effective medical treatment
Excimer laser (targeted UVB)
Ruxolitinib cream (new JAK inhibitor — FDA approved 2022)
Surgical options (split-skin grafting, melanocyte transfer) for stable vitiligo
Oral mini-pulse steroids (betamethasone) for progressing vitiligo — common in India
Cosmetic camouflage
prevention: Avoid chemical exposure (check rubber gloves for phenols)
affected_areas: Any body site (universal in severe cases)

skin_diseases.name: Melasma (Chloasma)
skin_diseases.description: Symmetric hyperpigmentation (dark patches) on face due to excess melanin production. Extremely prevalent in Indian women due to darker skin type, hormonal factors (contraceptives, pregnancy), and intense sun exposure. A major cosmetic concern in India.
causes: Hormonal changes: pregnancy, oral contraceptives, hormone therapy
Indian skin types (III-VI) have more melanocytes prone to hyperpigmentation
symptoms: Symmetric brown, grey-brown, or blue-grey patches
Most common on cheeks, forehead, upper lip, bridge of nose, chin
No texture change — just colour
Worsens dramatically in summer/sun
May improve in winter
No pain or itching
Three patterns: centrofacial (most common), malar, mandibular
treatments: Strict, lifelong sun protection: SPF 50+ PA+++ broad-spectrum physical/chemical sunscreen
Physical sun protection: hat, umbrella, avoid peak sun hours
Topical depigmenting agents: Hydroquinone 2-4% (gold standard) at night for 3-6 months
Combination: HQ + tretinoin 0.025-0.05% + topical steroid (Kligman's formula)
Azelaic acid 15-20% (safe in pregnancy, nursing)
Kojic acid 2-4%
Niacinamide 4-5%
Chemical peels (glycolic acid, trichloroacetic acid) — do carefully in Indian skin
Tranexamic acid (topical or oral) — increasingly popular in India
Laser: Q-switched Nd:YAG with caution (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation risk in Indian skin)
prevention: Daily SPF 50+ sunscreen year-round — MOST IMPORTANT step
Avoid OCP if melasma develops — switch to progesterone-only or non-hormonal contraception
Avoid lime juice on face in sun (phytophotodermatitis)
warning_signs: Exogenous ochronosis (paradoxical darkening from HQ overuse)

skin_diseases.name: Urticaria (Hives)
skin_diseases.description: Acute or chronic eruption of itchy wheals (hives) due to mast cell degranulation and histamine release. Very common in India — often triggered by food, medications, infections, or unknown causes in chronic urticaria (>6 weeks).
causes: Allergic: foods (seafood, nuts, eggs, milk very common in India), drugs (NSAIDs, aspirin, antibiotics)
Infections (viral, bacterial, parasitic — common in India)
Physical urticaria: cold, heat, pressure, vibration, exercise
Chronic urticaria: often autoimmune or unknown cause
symptoms: Pale pink or red raised wheals (hives) that are intensely itchy
Individual lesions appear and disappear within 24 hours
Wheals may be small or large, round or irregular
May join together
Angioedema (deeper swelling of lips, eyes, tongue, throat) in severe cases
Dermographism (wheals on stroking skin) in physical urticaria
treatments: Non-sedating antihistamines first line: cetirizine 10mg daily or fexofenadine 180mg daily
Doubling or quadrupling antihistamine dose in chronic urticaria if poorly controlled
Adding H2 blocker (ranitidine) may help
Omalizumab (anti-IgE biologic) for chronic urticaria unresponsive to antihistamines
Short course oral prednisolone for severe acute attacks
Epinephrine (adrenaline) injection for anaphylaxis — angioedema with throat involvement
affected_areas: Common on trunk, arms, legs, face
warning_signs: Swelling of lips, tongue, throat (angioedema — medical emergency)

skin_diseases.name: Seborrhoeic Dermatitis
skin_diseases.description: Chronic inflammatory condition affecting areas rich in sebaceous glands, causing greasy scales, redness, and dandruff. Very common in India, worsened by humidity. Affects scalp, face, and body folds.
symptoms: Dandruff: flaking, itching of scalp
Yellowish or white greasy scales
Redness
Common sites: scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, behind ears, chest
Cradle cap in infants (thick, greasy scalp scales)
May affect armpits, groin, beard area
Waxing and waning course
treatments: Medicated shampoos (use on scalp and affected skin areas): Ketoconazole 2%, selenium sulfide 1-2.5%, zinc pyrithione, coal tar, ciclopirox olamine
Leave on for 3-5 minutes before rinsing
Topical antifungal (ketoconazole cream) for facial involvement
Mild topical steroids (hydrocortisone) for acute flares
Topical calcineurin inhibitors for face (tacrolimus) to avoid steroid side effects
warning_signs: Severe SD in adults — screen for HIV
Parkinson's association — unusual if new onset in elderly

skin_diseases.name: Contact Dermatitis
skin_diseases.description: Skin inflammation from contact with irritants or allergens. Very common in India — occupational (farmers, construction workers, healthcare workers), cosmetic-induced (mehendi allergy to PPD, bindis, hair dye), and bindi/kumkum reactions are unique Indian presentations.
causes: Allergens: para-phenylenediamine (PPD) in black mehendi and hair dye — very common in India, nickel (jewellery), bindi adhesive, kumkum (Parthenium), rubber latex, fragrance, preservatives in cosmetics
Irritants: soaps, detergents, agriculture chemicals (pesticides — common in Indian farmers), cement (construction workers)
Plants: Parthenium hysterophorus (congress grass) — weed allergy extremely common in India
symptoms: Acute allergic: intense itch, red, vesicular, oozing rash at site of contact, 48-72h after exposure
Irritant: burning, stinging, redness immediately or hours after contact
Lichenification with chronic repeated exposure
Characteristic patterns: bindi forehead rash, kumkum neck rash, necklace pattern, forehead+neck+arms (Parthenium)
Hand eczema in healthcare workers and housewives
treatments: Remove and avoid the causative agent
Cool compresses and calamine lotion for comfort
Topical corticosteroids (hydrocortisone mild, betamethasone moderate-severe)
Oral antihistamines (cetirizine)
Oral prednisolone short course for severe reactions
Barrier creams for occupational exposure
Patch testing for diagnosis
prevention: Patch test before using new cosmetics
Use natural (plain) mehendi — avoid black mehendi with PPD
Wear protective gloves for occupational exposure

skin_diseases.name: Folliculitis
skin_diseases.description: Infection or inflammation of hair follicles. Extremely common in India due to heat, humidity, and sweating. Ranges from superficial folliculitis (barber's itch, shaving rash) to deep furuncles (boils) and carbuncles. S. aureus most common cause.
causes: Gram-negative folliculitis (in acne patients on antibiotics)
Predisposing: heat, humidity, tight clothing, friction, diabetes, obesity
symptoms: Superficial folliculitis: clusters of small pustules around hair follicles, itchy or tender
Furuncle (boil): deep, painful, hot, red, pus-filled nodule around single follicle
Carbuncle: multiple connected furuncles with multiple drainage points, systemic symptoms
Pseudofolliculitis: ingrown hair bumps in beard area after shaving
Pityrosporum folliculitis: monomorphic pustules on upper trunk, itchy
treatments: Superficial folliculitis: topical mupirocin or clindamycin lotion, antiseptic washes (chlorhexidine)
Furuncle: warm compresses (brings to head), incision and drainage when fluctuant
Carbuncle/recurring furuncles: oral antibiotics (flucloxacillin, cefalexin or co-amoxiclav for 7-10 days)
MRSA: doxycycline or co-trimoxazole (based on culture)
Pityrosporum: ketoconazole or itraconazole
Diabetes control critical for recurrent disease
prevention: Bathe daily, especially in humid weather
Use antiseptic soap in areas prone to folliculitis
Shave in direction of hair growth
Chlorhexidine body wash for decolonisation in recurrent disease
warning_signs: Recurrent boils — rule out diabetes, HIV, iron deficiency, S. aureus carriage

skin_diseases.name: Impetigo
skin_diseases.description: Highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection common in Indian children, especially in schools and slums during monsoon season. Honey-coloured crusted sores and blistering characterise the condition. S. aureus most common cause in India.
causes: Entry via minor skin breaks, insect bites, chickenpox sores
symptoms: Red sores that rupture quickly and form honey-coloured crusts
Satellite lesions from self-spread (auto-inoculation)
Mildly itchy
Bullous impetigo: large fluid-filled blisters (S. aureus toxin mediated)
Usually on face (around nose and mouth) and exposed skin
Lymphadenopathy nearby
treatments: Localised: Topical mupirocin ointment 3 times daily for 5-7 days OR fusidic acid cream
Extensive/bullous: Oral antibiotics: cefalexin 250-500mg 4 times daily for 7 days OR co-amoxiclav OR clindamycin
Gently clean crusts with soapy water before applying topical
MRSA impetigo: co-trimoxazole or doxycycline
prevention: Keep children home from school until sores healed or 48h post-antibiotic start
warning_signs: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (kidney complication after Strep impetigo)
MRSA suspected (not responding to standard antibiotics)

skin_diseases.name: Chickenpox (Varicella)
skin_diseases.description: Highly contagious viral illness presenting with characteristic itchy vesicular rash. Endemic in India with seasonal peaks (spring and monsoon). Unlike developed countries, widespread childhood vaccination not universal in India — outbreaks common. Risk of complications in adults, immunocompromised, and neonates.
causes: Highly contagious — airborne and direct contact
Infectious from 2 days before rash until all vesicles crusted (5-7 days post-rash)
symptoms: Prodrome: 1-2 days of fever, malaise, headache
Rash starts on face/scalp/trunk, spreads to extremities
Rapid progression: macule → papule → vesicle (dewdrop on red base) → pustule → crust
Different stages simultaneously — diagnostic
Intensely itchy
Oral mucosal ulcers possible
Mild fever throughout
Complications: bacterial superinfection, pneumonitis, encephalitis, Reye's (if given aspirin)
treatments: Symptomatic: calamine lotion, oral antihistamines (cetirizine/chlorpheniramine) for itch
Paracetamol for fever (NEVER aspirin — Reye's syndrome)
Keep nails trimmed short to prevent scratching/secondary infection
Oral acyclovir for adults (>12yr), immunocompromised, newborns, pregnant (800mg 5 times daily for 7 days — start within 24h of rash)
IV acyclovir for severe disease, encephalitis, immunocompromised
prevention: Varicella vaccine (highly effective — recommended in Indian Pediatric Society schedule)
Isolate infected individuals until all lesions crusted
Varicella-zoster immunoglobulin for high-risk contacts (immunocompromised, neonates, pregnant)

skin_diseases.name: Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
skin_diseases.description: Reactivation of latent Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) from dorsal root ganglia, causing painful dermatomal rash. Common in elderly Indians, immunocompromised, HIV-positive, and those on immunosuppressants. Can cause severe post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) — chronic pain lasting months/years.
causes: Reactivation of latent VZV from sensory ganglia
Triggers: immunosuppression (steroids, HIV, chemotherapy, malignancy), elderly, stress
symptoms: Prodromal pain, burning, itching in a band (dermatomal) — preceding rash by 2-3 days
Unilateral dermatomal erythema then grouped vesicles on red base
Does NOT cross midline
Intense pain — may precede or exceed rash severity
Most common: thoracic (trunk), trigeminal (face/eye)
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: rash on forehead + risk of eye damage
Ramsay Hunt syndrome: ear vesicles + facial palsy + hearing loss
Post-herpetic neuralgia: persistent burning pain after rash heals (older patients)
treatments: Antiviral: Oral valacyclovir 1000mg three times daily OR acyclovir 800mg five times daily for 7-10 days — start within 72h of rash for best effect
Pregabalin or gabapentin for neuropathic pain
Amitriptyline for PHN
Calamine lotion and analgesics (paracetamol, tramadol)
Ophthalmic involvement: urgent ophthalmologist referral + topical antiviral eye drops
prevention: Shingrix vaccine (recombinant — available in India for >50 years) highly effective
affected_areas: Trigeminal (V1 ophthalmic — forehead, eye, nose tip)
warning_signs: Eye involvement (herpes zoster ophthalmicus — needs urgent specialist care)

skin_diseases.name: Leprosy (Hansen's Disease)
skin_diseases.description: Chronic bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae, primarily affecting skin and peripheral nerves. India accounts for more than 50% of global leprosy cases. A major public health priority — under elimination programme. Reversible if detected and treated early; nerve damage is irreversible.
causes: Spread by respiratory droplets from multibacillary patients
Only 5% of exposed individuals develop disease (most are immune)
symptoms: Hypopigmented (pale) or erythematous (red) patches with LOSS OF SENSATION — key diagnostic feature
Single or few asymmetric lesions in tuberculoid leprosy (paucibacillary)
Multiple, symmetric, extensive lesions in lepromatous leprosy (multibacillary)
Peripheral nerve thickening (great auricular nerve, ulnar nerve palpable)
Clawing of fingers (ulnar nerve), foot drop (peroneal nerve)
Lagophthalmos (inability to close eyes — facial nerve)
Trophic ulcers on feet (anaesthetic feet)
Madarosis (loss of outer eyebrows) in lepromatous leprosy
Reactions (Type 1, Type 2 — ENL) can cause acute deterioration
treatments: WHO Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) — provided free by Government of India:
Paucibacillary (1-5 lesions): Rifampicin 600mg + Dapsone 100mg monthly supervised; Dapsone 100mg daily unsupervised for 6 months
Multibacillary (>5 lesions): Rifampicin 600mg + Clofazimine 300mg + Dapsone 100mg monthly supervised; Clofazimine 50mg + Dapsone 100mg daily for 12 months
Reactions: Type 1 — oral prednisolone; Type 2 (ENL) — thalidomide or clofazimine + prednisolone
Physiotherapy and footwear for nerve damage prevention
Reconstructive surgery for deformities
prevention: BCG vaccination in childhood offers partial protection
Early detection and treatment of cases
Contact examination and prophylactic rifampicin in some guidelines
warning_signs: Sudden increase in patches or nerve pain (Type 1 reaction)
Tender red nodules all over skin + fever + joint pain (Type 2/ENL reaction)
Worsening nerve function (needs urgent steroid treatment)

skin_diseases.name: Prickly Heat (Miliaria)
skin_diseases.description: Blocked eccrine sweat glands causing sweat retention and skin inflammation. Extremely common in India during hot and humid summers, monsoon season, and in infants. Often called 'ghamori' or 'prickly heat' in India.
symptoms: Miliaria crystallina: superficial clear vesicles like dew drops, no redness — breaks easily
Miliaria rubra (prickly heat): small red papules and vesicles, intensely itchy/prickly sensation, neck, trunk, intertriginous areas
Miliaria profunda (deep — less common): flesh-coloured papules, in repeated severe miliaria
Symptoms worse in heat, improve in cool environment
Babies: face, neck, upper trunk most affected
treatments: Move to cooler, air-conditioned environment
Cool water baths, loose cotton clothing
Calamine lotion (soothing)
Prickly heat powder (zinc oxide, talc-based) to absorb moisture — widely used in India
Mild hydrocortisone cream if severe inflammation
Avoid occlusive creams and ointments (worsen blockage)
prevention: Stay cool — fans, AC, cool baths
Keep skin dry, especially neck and skin folds
Prickly heat powder use in India is a traditional preventive measure

skin_diseases.name: Drug Rash (Drug Eruption)
skin_diseases.description: Skin reactions to medications — very common given the high medication use in India (poly-pharmacy, OTC NSAID/antibiotic overuse). Ranges from morbilliform (measles-like) rash to severe, life-threatening Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).
causes: Most common culprits in India: Co-trimoxazole, penicillin/amoxicillin (most common), NSAIDs (nimesulide, diclofenac), allopurinol, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin), anti-TB drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide)
Genetic variants (HLA-B*57:01 for nevirapine/abacavir; HLA-B*15:02 for carbamazepine SJS — common in South/SE Asians)
symptoms: Morbilliform rash (most common): symmetrical red blotchy rash starting on trunk and spreading to extremities, 1-2 weeks after starting drug
Urticaria: itchy hives (see Urticaria entry)
Fixed drug eruption (FDE): recurring red/dark oval patch at SAME site each time drug is taken — paracetamol, sulphonamides common cause in India
SJS: extensive blistering + mucosal (eye/mouth/genital) involvement, fever — <10% BSA skin loss
TEN: >30% BSA skin detachment — medical emergency with high mortality
treatments: Identify and STOP the causative drug immediately
Mild morbilliform/urticarial: antihistamines, topical corticosteroids, time

SJS/TEN: hospitalise urgently, aggressive wound care (like burns unit), IV fluids, ocular lubricants/ciclosporin eye drops, consider IVIG or ciclosporin systemically — avoid systemic steroids (controversial)
Alert patient to avoid drug permanently — medical alert bracelet if SJS/TEN
prevention: Careful prescribing — avoid drugs with high cross-reactivity in high-risk patients
Pharmacogenomic testing for HLA-B*15:02 in carbamazepine use in South Asian patients
Patient education about drug allergy signs
affected_areas: Mucous membranes in SJS/TEN (eyes, mouth, genitals)
Fixed sites in fixed drug eruption
warning_signs: Eye redness, pain, or discharge (mucosal involvement — SJS)
IMMEDIATELY STOP DRUG and go to hospital

skin_diseases.name: Warts (Verruca)
skin_diseases.description: Benign skin growths caused by HPV infection. Common in Indian children and young adults. Often cosmetically troublesome. Plantar warts (on soles) very painful. Genital warts are sexually transmitted.
causes: Walking barefoot in public areas (plantar warts)
symptoms: Common warts: rough, cauliflower-like, flesh-coloured bumps with black dots (thrombosed capillaries) on hands/fingers
Plantar warts: flat, painful, inward-growing with black dots on soles — painful on walking
Flat warts: smooth, small, numerous — face and dorsum of hands in children
Periungual warts: around and under nails
Filiform warts: finger-like projections on face
Usually painless except plantar warts
treatments: Most resolve spontaneously in 2 years in healthy individuals
Topical salicylic acid (12-40%): apply daily after paring dead skin — mainstay of treatment
Cryotherapy: liquid nitrogen freezing every 2-3 weeks — clinic procedure
Immunotherapy: topical diphencyprone, imiquimod cream 5% (especially genital warts)
Surgical removal: curettage + electrodesiccation
Intralesional bleomycin or MMR vaccine injection for resistant warts
prevention: Avoid walking barefoot in public shower/pool areas
HPV vaccine (Gardasil/Cervarix) prevents genital warts and cervical cancer — recommended in India for girls 9-14 years
warning_signs: Warts in genital area — STI screen and sexual health assessment

skin_diseases.name: Hyperpigmentation / Post-Inflammatory Hyperpigmentation (PIH)
skin_diseases.description: Dark marks left after skin inflammation (acne, eczema, injury). Extremely common in Indian skin (phototypes III-VI) as darker skin has more reactive melanocytes. Often more troubling to patients than the original condition. Also includes dark underarms, dark knuckles, neck darkening (Acanthosis Nigricans — marker for insulin resistance).
causes: Post-inflammatory: acne, eczema, insect bites, cuts, burns all trigger melanocyte overactivation in Indian skin
Acanthosis nigricans: insulin resistance (obesity, diabetes, PCOS), medications (steroids, OCP)
Friction (dark underarms, dark neck from rubbing)
Chemical irritants (deodorants with alcohol in underarms)
symptoms: Dark brown to black macules or patches at site of previous inflammation
Flat, no texture change
Worsens with sun exposure
Acanthosis Nigricans: velvety, dark, thickened skin in folds (neck, underarms, groin) — marker for insulin resistance
Dark underarms from friction and deodorant irritation
Dark inner thighs from friction
Dark knuckles (Dowling-Degos syndrome in some)
treatments: Sun protection (SPF 30-50 daily) — essential and most effective step
Topical depigmenting: niacinamide (4-5%), kojic acid, azelaic acid, alpha-arbutin, vitamin C serum
Hydroquinone 2-4% for persistent PIH (avoid long-term)
Retinoids (tretinoin at night)
Chemical exfoliants: glycolic acid, lactic acid, mandelic acid (gentler for Indian skin)
Acanthosis Nigricans: treat underlying insulin resistance (weight loss, metformin for diabetes/PCOS)
Dark underarms: avoid harsh deodorants, lose weight, treat fungal/bacterial infections
prevention: Treat acne/eczema early to prevent PIH
Avoid picking or irritating inflamed skin
Treat insulin resistance (lifestyle modifications, weight management)
warning_signs: Acanthosis Nigricans: evaluate for diabetes, PCOS
Rapid onset widespread darkening — check thyroid, adrenal disease

skin_diseases.name: Cellulitis
skin_diseases.description: Bacterial infection of deeper skin layers (dermis and subcutaneous tissue). Common in India — particularly in lower limbs with lymphoedema, filariasis, diabetes. Can spread rapidly and become life-threatening if untreated.
causes: Entry via: cuts, wounds, insect bites, athlete's foot, toe-web infections, leg ulcers
Risk factors: diabetes (very common in India), obesity, leg oedema, filariasis lymphoedema
symptoms: Rapidly spreading red, warm, swollen, painful area of skin
Well-demarcated (erysipelas) or poorly demarcated borders
Systemic features: fever, chills, malaise (in moderate-severe)
Red streaks spreading up limb (lymphangitis — ascending lymph involvement)
Blisters, purpura in severe disease
Lower leg most commonly affected
treatments: Oral antibiotics for mild-moderate: cefalexin or co-amoxiclav (7-14 days)
IV antibiotics for severe/rapidly spreading: benzylpenicillin or flucloxacillin; ceftriaxone for penicillin allergy
MRSA suspected: IV vancomycin or oral clindamycin/co-trimoxazole
Elevate limb
Mark the border with pen to monitor spread
Treat portal of entry (tinea pedis, wounds)
Diabetic foot: multidisciplinary care
prevention: Prophylactic low-dose penicillin for >3 episodes per year
warning_signs: Necrotising fasciitis (rapidly spreading, severe pain, skin discolouration, crepitus) — surgical emergency
Red streaks tracking up limb (septicaemia risk)
Orbital cellulitis (facial cellulitis near eye — involves vision risk)

skin_diseases.name: Photodermatitis / Sunburn
skin_diseases.description: Abnormal skin reactions to ultraviolet radiation. Common in India due to intense sun exposure. Includes PMLE (Polymorphous Light Eruption), photoallergic contact dermatitis (due to lime juice, perfumes, drugs + sun), and simple sunburn. Phytophotodermatitis from lime juice + sun is very common in rural India.
causes: PMLE: abnormal immune response to UV radiation
Phytophotodermatitis: furocoumarin-containing plants (lime, lemon, mango peel, coriander, celery) + UV
Photoallergic contact dermatitis: sunscreens, fragrances, certain drugs + UV
Phototoxic drugs: doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, NSAIDs, amiodarone, hydrochlorothiazide + sun
Simple sunburn: excessive UV without protection
symptoms: PMLE: itchy papules, vesicles, or plaques on sun-exposed areas 30 min-24h after sun exposure

Phytophotodermatitis (lime rash): blistering with linear/splash patterns exactly where lime juice contacted skin, hyperpigmentation after healing — classic after squeezing lime in sun at roadside stalls
Sunburn: acute erythema, pain, peeling
Drug phototoxicity: exaggerated sunburn reaction beyond sun exposure area
treatments: PMLE: sun avoidance, protective clothing, high SPF, topical corticosteroids for active eruption
Phytophotodermatitis: cool compresses, topical steroid, treat PIH afterwards
Sunburn: cool water, emollient, ibuprofen for pain, aloe vera
Drug photosensitivity: reduce or avoid sun exposure while on drug
prevention: Wash off lime/plant juices from skin before sun exposure
Know photosensitising side effects of medications
warning_signs: Persistent photosensitivity even without sun (check medications, SLE)

skin_diseases.name: Alopecia (Hair Loss)
skin_diseases.scientific_name: Alopecia areata / Androgenetic alopecia / Telogen effluvium
skin_diseases.description: Hair loss conditions are extremely common in India. Androgenetic alopecia (male/female pattern baldness) most prevalent, followed by telogen effluvium (stress/nutritional shedding — very common post-COVID), and alopecia areata (autoimmune patchy hair loss). Nutritional causes (iron, B12, Vitamin D, protein deficiency) very common in vegetarian Indian population.
causes: Telogen effluvium: major triggers in India: nutritional deficiency (iron, B12, Vitamin D, protein), thyroid disease (very common), post-COVID hair loss, post-partum, severe illness, emotional stress
Alopecia areata: autoimmune attack on hair follicles, HLA-associated
Tinea capitis: fungal infection — especially in children
Scarring alopecia: lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus
symptoms: Pattern baldness: gradual recession and thinning in characteristic patterns (temples, crown in men; diffuse thinning in women)
Telogen effluvium: diffuse shedding, positive pull test, 2-4 months after triggering event
Alopecia areata: one or more smooth, round bald patches; exclamation mark hairs at margin; nail pitting associated
Tinea capitis: scaly scalp patch with hair breakage, +/- kerion (boggy mass)
Trichotillomania: irregular patches in reachable areas
treatments: Androgenetic: Minoxidil 5% solution/foam topically for men and women, Finasteride 1mg daily (men only), hair transplant
Telogen effluvium: identify and treat cause (iron/B12/VitD supplementation — VERY IMPORTANT in India), patient reassurance (reversible)
Alopecia areata: topical high-potency steroids, intralesional triamcinolone, oral mini-pulse steroids, topical diphencyprone, JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, ruxolitinib) for extensive disease
Tinea capitis: oral antifungals (griseofulvin, terbinafine) — topical alone insufficient
prevention: Adequate nutrition — iron-rich foods, B12 (eggs, dairy, or supplement if vegan)
Gentle hair care (avoid tight braids, heat styling)
warning_signs: Tinea capitis with kerion (needs systemic antifungals urgently)
Associated autoimmune disease (thyroid, vitiligo, atopy in alopecia areata)

skin_diseases.name: Intertrigo
skin_diseases.description: Inflammation of opposing skin surfaces (skin folds) due to friction, moisture, and often secondary candidal or bacterial infection. Extremely common in India due to heat and humidity, especially in overweight individuals, diabetics, and infants.
causes: Risk factors: obesity, diabetes, incontinence, immobility
symptoms: Red, raw, moist, macerated skin in folds
Satellite lesions (small papules/pustules around main rash — suggests Candida)
Itching, burning, pain
Foul odour possible
Groin, underarms, beneath breasts, abdominal folds, perianal
Infants: buttock fold, neck rash
treatments: Keep area clean and dry
Topical antifungal (clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily for Candida)
Antifungal powder (miconazole-based) — very useful in India's humid climate
Nystatin powder or cream for Candida in infants
Hydrocortisone 1% cream with antifungal for inflammation (short-term)
Whitfield's ointment (benzoic acid + salicylic acid) for ringworm-type intertrigo
Absorb moisture with zinc oxide paste or antifungal powder
Oral fluconazole for extensive/recurrent Candidal intertrigo
prevention: Keep folds clean and dry after bathing
Dry folds thoroughly (hair dryer on cool setting)
Use antifungal powder in folds in hot weather
warning_signs: Not responding to antifungals — recurrent Candida suggests diabetes or immunosuppression

skin_diseases.name: Rosacea
skin_diseases.description: Chronic inflammatory facial condition causing persistent redness, flushing, visible blood vessels, and acne-like bumps. Common globally, increasingly diagnosed in Indian patients. Sun, heat, spicy food, and alcohol are classic triggers.
causes: Triggers: UV, heat, spicy food, alcohol, stress
symptoms: Persistent central facial redness
Flushing episodes
Papules and pustules (no blackheads)
Telangiectasia (visible capillaries)
Burning/stinging sensation
Rhinophyma (bulbous nose) in severe cases
Eye redness (ocular rosacea)
treatments: Topical metronidazole gel 0.75-1% twice daily
Topical ivermectin 1% cream once daily
Azelaic acid 15-20%
Oral doxycycline 40mg MR once daily (anti-inflammatory dose)
IPL/laser for telangiectasia
Brimonidine gel for redness
Sun protection SPF 50+ essential
prevention: Avoid hot drinks and spicy food if triggers
warning_signs: Eye pain or vision changes (ocular rosacea)

skin_diseases.name: Pityriasis Rosea
skin_diseases.description: Self-limiting skin rash characterised by a 'herald patch' followed by widespread oval scaly patches in a Christmas-tree distribution. Thought to be caused by HHV-6/7 viral reactivation. Common in young adults, usually resolves in 6-12 weeks.
causes: Possibly triggered by certain medications (gold, metronidazole, captopril)
symptoms: Herald patch: single oval salmon-pink scaly plaque (2-5cm) on trunk, 1-2 weeks before widespread eruption
Widespread secondary rash: numerous smaller oval patches with collarette scaling
Christmas-tree distribution along rib lines
Mild itching
Usually trunk, arms, thighs (spares face, hands, feet)
Self-resolves in 6-12 weeks
treatments: Usually reassurance — self-limiting
Emollients for dryness and comfort
Mild topical corticosteroids if itchy
Oral antihistamines (cetirizine) for itch
UVB phototherapy for widespread itchy cases
Sun exposure may hasten resolution (natural UVB)
Acyclovir (limited evidence, may shorten course in early, severe cases)

skin_diseases.name: Lichen Planus
skin_diseases.description: Chronic autoimmune inflammatory condition affecting skin, nails, mucous membranes, and scalp. Characterized by violaceous flat-topped papules with a lacy white surface pattern. Hepatitis C association important.
causes: Autoimmune T-cell attack on basal keratinocytes
symptoms: Flat-topped polygonal violaceous (purple) papules
Intense itching
Wickham's striae (white lacy lines on lesion surface)
Distribution: flexor wrists, lower legs, lower back, genitals
Koebner phenomenon (new lesions at trauma sites)
Oral: white reticular pattern or painful erosions
Nail: thinning, ridging, pterygium formation
treatments: Potent topical corticosteroids (betamethasone, clobetasol) — first line
Oral prednisolone for widespread acute disease
Topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus (oral/genital LP, face)
Hydroxychloroquine 200-400mg daily
Oral acitretin (retinoid) for resistant cases
NB-UVB phototherapy

skin_diseases.name: Bullous Pemphigoid
skin_diseases.description: Autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease — the most common autoimmune bullous disorder globally. Affects predominantly elderly patients (>60 years). Large, tense blisters on normal or urticarial (hive-like) skin. Better prognosis than pemphigus vulgaris.
causes: Anti-BP180 and anti-BP230 antibodies attacking hemidesmosomal proteins
Drug-induced (gliptins/DPP4 inhibitors, furosemide — important in India as gliptins widely used)
symptoms: Prodrome: urticarial or eczematous pruritic plaques (weeks to months)
Tense blisters (thick wall, do NOT rupture easily) on urticarial base
Nikolsky sign NEGATIVE (differentiates from pemphigus)
Axillae, inner thighs, lower abdomen
Mucous membranes rarely involved
Very elderly patients typically
treatments: Superpotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol) — for localised disease
Oral prednisolone (0.5mg/kg) for widespread disease
Doxycycline + Niacinamide (alternative, less immunosuppression)
Azathioprine or Mycophenolate mofetil (steroid-sparing)
Rituximab for refractory disease
Stop suspected drugs (check gliptins)

skin_diseases.name: Granuloma Annulare
skin_diseases.description: Benign self-limiting skin condition characterised by ring-shaped smooth papules or plaques, usually on extremities. Associated with diabetes in some cases. Often confused with ringworm (tinea) but has no scale and no fungal cause.
symptoms: Ring-shaped collection of smooth skin-coloured or slightly erythematous papules
No scaling (differentiates from ringworm)
Usually on dorsal hands, fingers, feet, ankles
Localised (young people) or generalised (associated with diabetes, older patients)
Usually asymptomatic
treatments: Localised: often self-resolves within 2 years — reassurance
Potent topical corticosteroids under occlusion
Intralesional triamcinolone injection
Cryotherapy
Phototherapy for generalised disease
warning_signs: Generalised disease in middle-aged/elderly — screen for diabetes

skin_diseases.name: Erythema Multiforme
skin_diseases.description: Acute immune-mediated skin condition with characteristic target lesions. Most often triggered by herpes simplex virus (HSV) or Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Severe form (Stevens-Johnson Syndrome) involves mucosal surfaces.
causes: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 or 2) — most common trigger (70% of cases)
symptoms: Target (iris) lesions: three concentric zones (central dark area, lighter ring, outer red ring)
Hands and feet most common (then spreads)
Mild EM Minor: no mucosal involvement
EM Major: mucosal involvement (oral/eye/genital) — overlap with SJS
Mild itching or burning
treatments: Remove triggering drug or treat underlying infection
Symptomatic: antihistamines, topical corticosteroids (mild)
Oral acyclovir/valacyclovir if HSV-triggered (prevent recurrence)
Oral steroid short course for severe EM
EM Major: hospital admission, wound care, ophthalmic involvement
prevention: Prophylactic antiviral (acyclovir/valacyclovir) for recurrent HSV-triggered EM
warning_signs: Mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals) — overlap SJS

skin_diseases.name: Dermatitis Herpetiformis
skin_diseases.description: Intensely itchy blistering rash associated with coeliac disease (gluten sensitivity). IgA deposits in dermal papillae. Very rare but important to diagnose as it indicates underlying gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Responds dramatically to gluten-free diet.
causes: IgA antibodies triggered by gluten (gliadin) deposition in skin
All patients have gluten-sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease) even if asymptomatic bowel
symptoms: Intensely itchy grouped papules and vesicles
Symmetrical distribution: elbows (extensor), knees, buttocks, scalp, back
So itchy lesions are often excoriated before vesicles seen
GI symptoms of coeliac disease (may be absent)
Associated thyroid disease
treatments: Strict lifelong gluten-free diet (cornerstone)
Dapsone 25-100mg daily — dramatic response within 24-72 hours (diagnostic and therapeutic)
Dapsone side effects: haemolysis (check G6PD before starting), methaemoglobinaemia
prevention: Strict gluten-free diet prevents and controls disease
warning_signs: Associated lymphoma (rare, with poorly controlled disease/non-adherent diet)

skin_diseases.name: Tinea Unguium (Onychomycosis)
skin_diseases.description: Fungal infection of the nails — very common. Most commonly affects toenails. Causes unsightly thickened, discoloured, crumbling nails. Requires prolonged antifungal treatment. Common in India due to exposure to moisture and shared footwear.
causes: Dermatophytes: T. rubrum (most common), T. mentagrophytes
Risk: diabetes, poor circulation, trauma, tinea pedis, shared footwear/public showers
symptoms: Yellow, white, or brown discolouration of nail
Thickening of nail plate
Subungual hyperkeratosis (debris under nail)
Crumbling, brittle nail
Onycholysis (nail lifting from nail bed)
Usually painless unless very thick
Toenails most common
treatments: Topical alone rarely effective for nail — for superficial or very mild: Amorolfine 5% nail lacquer
Oral antifungals required: Terbinafine 250mg daily for 6 weeks (fingernails) to 12-16 weeks (toenails) — most effective
Itraconazole 200mg daily for 12 weeks OR pulse therapy
Laser treatment (adjunct)
Monitor liver function on long-term oral antifungals
prevention: Wear breathable socks and well-ventilated shoes
Avoid walking barefoot in public areas
Treat tinea pedis promptly (seeds nail infection)
warning_signs: Rapid spread to multiple nails in diabetics

skin_diseases.name: Lupus Erythematosus (Cutaneous)
skin_diseases.description: Autoimmune skin manifestations of lupus. Can occur with or without systemic lupus (SLE). Classic butterfly (malar) rash over cheeks is iconic. Discoid lupus causes permanent scarring. Photosensitivity is a hallmark.
causes: Autoimmune — Type III hypersensitivity, complement activation
Drugs can trigger: hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline
symptoms: Malar (butterfly) rash: erythema over cheeks and nose bridge, sparing nasolabial folds
Photosensitivity (worsens with sun)
Discoid lupus: scarring plaques with follicular plugging — permanent hair loss
Subacute CLE: annular/psoriasiform plaques on sun-exposed areas
Systemic: joint pain, fatigue, renal, CNS involvement in SLE
treatments: Strict photoprotection: SPF 50+ broad-spectrum sunscreen daily, protective clothing
Topical corticosteroids
Topical tacrolimus (especially face)
Hydroxychloroquine 200-400mg daily (cornerstone for CLE — reduces flares, protects from progression to SLE)
Oral prednisolone for acute severe flares
Dapsone, mepacrine for refractory CLE
prevention: Strict sun avoidance and protection — ESSENTIAL
warning_signs: Systemic symptoms: joint pain, renal symptoms, fatigue (consider SLE)

skin_diseases.name: Pemphigus Vulgaris
skin_diseases.description: Severe potentially life-threatening autoimmune blistering disease. Higher prevalence in South Asians (India, Pakistan) and those of Jewish/Mediterranean descent. Oral mucosal involvement almost universal and often precedes skin disease by months.
causes: Anti-desmoglein 1 and 3 autoantibodies disrupting keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis)
HLA-DR4 and DRw6 association (common in South Asians)
symptoms: Painful oral ulcers/erosions — FIRST symptom (months before skin)
Flaccid (thin-walled, easily rupturing) blisters on normal-appearing skin
Erosions (blisters rupture, leaving raw painful areas)
Positive Nikolsky sign (lateral pressure extends lesion)
Koebner phenomenon
Any mucosal surface (oesophagus, conjunctiva, genitals)
Systemic: fever, weight loss in severe disease
treatments: Oral prednisolone 1-1.5mg/kg/day (initial high dose)
Rituximab (anti-CD20 biologic) — now first-line for moderate-severe (dramatically improved outcomes)
Azathioprine or Mycophenolate mofetil (steroid-sparing)
Dapsone (adjunct)
IVIG for refractory disease
Topical mouthwash (dexamethasone) for oral disease
Wound care — sterile dressings for erosions

skin_diseases.name: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis / Periorbital Dermatitis
skin_diseases.description: Inflammation around the eyes from atopic, contact, or seborrhoeic causes. Common and often difficult to treat due to thin delicate periorbital skin. Steroid misuse around eyes causes serious complications (glaucoma, cataract).
causes: Allergic contact: eye drops (neomycin), cosmetics, eye makeup, nail varnish (applied by touching eyes)
Irritant contact: cleansers, shampoo, rubbing eyes
symptoms: Red, scaly, itchy skin around eyes
Swelling of eyelids
Lichenification (thickening from chronic scratching)
May have papules or vesicles
Bilateral or unilateral depending on cause
treatments: Identify and remove cause (patch test if allergic)
Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.03% or pimecrolimus) — PREFERRED for periorbital — no steroid risk
Very mild topical steroid (hydrocortisone 1%) short-term ONLY — risk of glaucoma/cataract
Antihistamines (systemic) for itch
Cold compress
Gentle fragrance-free moisturiser
warning_signs: Never use potent steroids around eyes without ophthalmologist guidance (glaucoma risk)
Vesicular periorbital rash (herpes zoster ophthalmicus — URGENT)

skin_diseases.name: Morphea (Localised Scleroderma)
skin_diseases.description: Autoimmune skin condition causing localised fibrosis and sclerosis of skin. NOT the same as systemic sclerosis. Presents as firm, ivory-white or yellow plaques. Usually limited to skin without internal organ involvement.
causes: Trauma, radiation (radiation morphea), infections (Borrelia — in Lyme endemic areas)
symptoms: Early: violaceous/lilac ring around expanding lesions
Established: central ivory-white or yellow firm plaques
Skin feels hard and tight
May cause restricted joint movement (linear morphea)
Usually asymptomatic unless functional limitation
Linear morphea en coup de sabre (forehead to scalp — frontal)
treatments: Active early phase: potent/superpotent topical steroids
NB-UVB or UVA-1 phototherapy (very effective)
Methotrexate ± oral prednisolone for extensive/linear forms (especially in children)
Calcipotriol cream
Physical therapy (if contractures)
warning_signs: Linear morphea in children (may cause limb growth discrepancy)

skin_diseases.name: Sebaceous Cyst (Epidermoid Cyst)
skin_diseases.description: Common benign subcutaneous cyst containing keratin material. Present as firm, smooth, skin-coloured lumps usually with a central punctum. Often infected requiring incision and drainage. Very common finding in dermatological practice in India.
symptoms: Smooth, round, firm subcutaneous lump
Central punctum (pore opening)
Skin-coloured or slightly yellowish
Moves with overlying skin
Cheesy odorous material if ruptured
Painful if infected (hot, red, swollen)
treatments: Uninfected: surgical excision with cyst wall (to prevent recurrence)
Infected: Incision and drainage first; excise after infection settles
Intralesional triamcinolone for inflamed cyst (without infection)
warning_signs: Rapid growth (consider lipoma, lymph node, or malignancy)
Overlying skin changes suggesting malignant transformation (very rare)

skin_diseases.name: Keloids and Hypertrophic Scars
skin_diseases.description: Abnormal fibrous tissue response to skin injury. Keloids extend beyond original wound boundaries; hypertrophic scars remain within wound. Extremely common in Indians and Africans (darker phototypes). Major cosmetic concern. Piercings, acne, surgery, burns are common causes.
causes: Aberrant wound healing with excess collagen
More common in dark skin (phototypes IV-VI)
Predisposing sites: ear, chest, shoulders, jaw
Triggers: ear piercing, acne, surgery, burns, BCG vaccination scar
symptoms: Keloid: firm, rubbery, raised scar extending BEYOND original wound
Hypertrophic scar: raised scar within wound boundaries, may regress
Pruritus (itching) or pain in keloid
Cosmetically disturbing
May restrict movement if over joint
treatments: Intralesional triamcinolone injections every 4-6 weeks (mainstay of treatment)
Silicone gel sheets (daily wear for 3-6 months)
Pressure therapy
Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen)
Laser (pulsed-dye laser, CO2)
Surgical excision + immediate adjuvant treatment (steroid injection or radiotherapy) — excision alone causes recurrence/larger keloid in keloid-prone individuals
prevention: Avoid unnecessary piercings and cosmetic surgery in keloid-prone individuals
Silicone sheets immediately post-surgery in susceptible individuals
warning_signs: Rapidly growing keloid with ulceration (rare malignant change)

skin_diseases.name: Tinea Capitis (Scalp Ringworm)
skin_diseases.description: Fungal infection of scalp and hair shafts. Very common in Indian children. Causes scalp scaling, hair loss (alopecia), and occasionally inflammatory kerion. Requires systemic (oral) antifungals — topical alone is insufficient.
causes: Trichophyton violaceum and T. rubrum (endothrix — common in India)
Spread by shared combs, hats, pillows, barber tools
symptoms: Scaly patches on scalp ± hair breakage
Partial alopecia (hair breaks at surface — 'black dot' tinea)
Itching
Kerion: inflammatory boggy swelling (immune response to fungus) — painful, pus-filled, causes scarring alopecia if untreated
Enlarged posterior lymph nodes
treatments: Oral antifungals (topical alone ineffective for tinea capitis)
Griseofulvin (traditional but still widely used in India) 10-20mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks with fatty meal
Terbinafine 4-6 weeks (T. rubrum and T. violaceum) — preferred for dermatophyte
Itraconazole pulse therapy
Antifungal shampoo (ketoconazole) reduces transmission but not curative alone
Kerion: oral antifungals + oral prednisolone (to reduce inflammation and prevent scarring)
prevention: Not sharing combs, hats, towels, pillow cases
Check and treat household contacts and pets
warning_signs: Kerion (boggy painful swelling) — needs urgent oral antifungal + steroid to prevent scarring alopecia

skin_diseases.name: Nail Psoriasis
skin_diseases.description: Psoriasis affecting the nails causing pitting, onycholysis, and subungual hyperkeratosis. Occurs in ~50% of psoriasis patients. Associated with psoriatic arthritis. Can cause significant functional impairment and cosmetic distress.
causes: Psoriasis affecting nail matrix and nail bed
symptoms: Nail pitting (small depressions — involvement of proximal nail matrix)
Oil-drop (salmon patch) discolouration
Onycholysis (nail separating from bed)
Subungual hyperkeratosis (thickening under nail)
Splinter haemorrhages
Beau's lines
In psoriatic arthritis: DIP joint involvement with nail disease
treatments: Topical corticosteroids under nail fold (potent, e.g., betamethasone)
Calcipotriol cream applied to nail folds
Intralesional triamcinolone injections into nail matrix
Systemic treatments (methotrexate, biologics) for severe nail psoriasis with skin/joint disease
Tazarotene gel (retinoid) topical
warning_signs: DIP joint pain/swelling with nail disease (psoriatic arthritis)
Nail destruction with significant functional loss

skin_diseases.name: Neurodermatitis (Lichen Simplex Chronicus)
skin_diseases.description: Thickened, leathery skin from chronic repetitive scratching or rubbing. The itch-scratch cycle becomes self-perpetuating. Very common in India — stress, anxiety, and atopic tendency are predisposing factors.
causes: Insect bite reaction that becomes self-perpetuating
Notalgia paraesthetica (back itch from nerve entrapment)
symptoms: Well-circumscribed plaque of thick, leathery (lichenified) skin
Exaggerated skin markings
Intense itching — worse at night and with stress
Common sites: nape of neck (women), shins, scalp, ankles, genital area
Patient often scratches during sleep
treatments: Break itch-scratch cycle
Potent topical corticosteroids (betamethasone) under occlusion
Tacrolimus or pimecrolimus (calcineurin inhibitors)
Oral antihistamines (especially sedating at night: chlorpheniramine)
Topical doxepin (anti-itch, limited availability)
Intralesional triamcinolone for resistant lesions
Capsaicin cream
Gabapentin or pregabalin for neuropathic itch

skin_diseases.name: Acanthosis Nigricans
skin_diseases.description: Hyperpigmented, velvety thickening of skin in body folds associated with insulin resistance. Extremely common in India given the high prevalence of obesity, PCOS, and type 2 diabetes. A cutaneous marker of metabolic disease.
causes: Insulin resistance (most common cause in India): obesity, T2DM, PCOS, metabolic syndrome
Malignant (rare): gastrointestinal cancer — in older patients without obesity
symptoms: Velvety, hyperpigmented skin thickening in body folds
Neck (posterior, lateral), axillae, groin, elbow, knee folds
May have skin tags in same areas
Gradual onset in metabolic causes
Can be extensive over large areas
treatments: Treat underlying cause (most important): insulin resistance → weight loss, metformin for diabetes/PCOS
Cosmetic: topical tretinoin 0.025-0.05%, topical salicylic acid, keratolytics
Chemical peels for cosmetic improvement
Urea-based creams
warning_signs: Acanthosis nigricans in lean, older patient without known metabolic cause (paraneoplastic — investigate for GI cancer)

skin_diseases.name: Milia
skin_diseases.description: Small white cysts (1-2mm) containing keratin, often on the face. Primary milia are spontaneous; secondary milia occur after skin trauma, burns, blistering disorders. Common cosmetic concern especially in newborns and young adults.
causes: Secondary: burns, blistering disorders, topical steroids, trauma
Neonatal milia: retention of keratin in follicles (resolves spontaneously)
symptoms: Multiple tiny (1-2mm) white or yellowish firm dome-shaped cysts
Face: cheeks, nose, eyelids, forehead
No inflammation or pain
Neonatal: resolve spontaneously within weeks
treatments: Neonatal: no treatment needed (self-resolving)
Adults: extraction with sterile needle or comedone extractor (by trained person)
Topical retinoids (tretinoin) improve skin cell turnover and prevent recurrence
Chemical peels
Not to be squeezed — can leave marks
warning_signs: Secondary milia after burns or blistering disease — treat underlying condition first

skin_diseases.name: Lipodermatosclerosis / Venous Eczema
skin_diseases.description: Skin changes from chronic venous insufficiency. Common in elderly, obese patients with varicose veins or DVT. Presents as red-brown scaly patches around inner ankle/lower leg. Can lead to venous leg ulcers.
causes: Chronic venous hypertension from varicose veins, DVT, or venous incompetence
Gravity-dependent fluid leads to haemosiderin deposits and skin changes
symptoms: Red-brown, scaly, itchy patches around inner ankle and lower third of leg
Oedema (ankle swelling)
Haemosiderin pigmentation (brown staining)
Lipodermatosclerosis: fibrotic, hard 'inverted champagne bottle' appearance
Venous leg ulcers (open wounds, usually medial malleolus)
treatments: Compression therapy (key treatment) — compression bandaging or stockings grade II-III
Topical corticosteroids for eczema component
Emollients for dry skin
